utterances.text: Just so you're under no misapprehension about the position you're in here, if any party to one of these cases wishes to bring expert evidence, then they're free to do that, but there are certain rules apply about producing reports, and so on. It's not your expertise that is the issue here today, otherwise there would have been a report prepared. Our concern is with the factual investigations you've carried out. As I understand it, you've already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, did you have occasion to meet and talk to many Serb refugees from Croatia, for instance, at any time?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Yes, in 1995 I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Well, they were recounting on videotape, because I was also filming them, their -- how and why they were expelled from Croatia, what was done to them, and they -- I don't know if I could assess right now all of the conclusions that I drew from that, but it was clear that there was a planned -- a pattern of racial persecution against the Serbian population of Croatia. That's -- that's clear from any -- okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Lituchy. Thank you. Let's focus on -- this is what -- let's focus on Kosovo, since that's what we're dealing with. Now, what do you base your knowledge on with respect to the events in Kosovo and Metohija, your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything I could base it on that's more important than my interviews of refugees from Kosovo. There's nothing -- there is no information, there's no hard evidence that I could rely on, or any information at all, for that matter, that I would rely on, I think that would override or take precedence over the information I obtained from the refugees who were expelled or persecuted from Kosovo. That would be the basis. That's the most important basis of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the conversations that you mentioned you had in 1999 immediately after the NATO pact aggression; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Yes. That was in --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you conduct those conversations? Where did you talk to the refugees from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: I conducted interviews with these refugees in Belgrade and also in the suburbs of Belgrade, northern suburbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the national structure of the refugees that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Our delegation as a whole interviewed Serbian refugees. I did not do the Serbian interviews, but I personally conducted the interviews with Roma refugees, Egyptian refugees, with Albanian refugees, and subsequently with a Jewish refugee as well. Let's see. Am I missing any -- oh, members of our delegation also interviewed Turkish -- Yugoslav Turks who were refugees, but I didn't conduct those -- those interviews.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say delegations or groups, who made up that group? How many of you were there? The names aren't that important but how many members did that group number, the one that conducted the interviews?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: There were approximately 16 of us who travelled for two weeks in -- around the -- around Serbia, around Yugoslavia, observing damage during -- following the bombing or during the bombing, and a number of us conducted interviews, but I conducted probably the most of the -- most of the interviews. This is something we planned to do prior to our departure, because we wanted to learn the reasons for the -- for what had happened to these refugees and the specifics, the specific details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Lituchy, to the best of your knowledge and following on from what you've just said and the information that stems from those interviews, is there a common cause that made these people leave Kosovo regardless of their national or religious affiliation, that is to say regardless of whether they were Albanians, Roma, Egyptians, Serbs? Is there a common denominator, a common or general cause for them to leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Well, there were two primary causes, I would say, and two secondary causes, but the -- if -- that's the first part of my answer. The second part of my answer would be that, is there a common denominator? I would say that there is perhaps one common denominator as a cause of the expulsion of all of these national groups and as well as Albanians from Kosovo -- all of the national groups were to one extent or another persecuted and expelled, and the main cause was KLA, the Kosovo Liberation Army's use of terrorism against these national groups. That's the one common denominator, although there are other causes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell me, in what way were you able to contact those people, come into contact with them?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: The -- I organised the delegation. I organised the interviews, but I had a lot of help from my contacts in Belgrade, particularly my contacts with the Roma federation, and they were extremely helpful in -- in providing the logistics to hold these, to make these interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness said that there were other causes, and he should tell us what the other causes are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one of the -- one of the -- the other one of the two primary causes from the interviews, and I'm basing this purely on my own investigation, was the bombing, the NATO bombing. That's -- I mean, that's -- in many cases that's why people had to flee. They had to flee bombing. Of course that's not -- that's not a common denominator. Not everybody fled because of the bombing, but everybody did flee -- who did flee because of Kosovo Liberation Army terrorism. The two secondary causes, I think, that were very important for the refugee crisis in June of 1999 were, first of all, the failure of KFOR forces, and I suppose also UNMIK, to provide security for non-Albanians and -- non-Albanian nationalities and for those Albanians who may not have been members of the KLA. Finally, a fourth reason, at least as far as I know and from -- from my investigation, is that the -- the absence of -- this is something that was told to us especially by Roma refugees, that once the Yugoslav army and police forces left Kosovo, the people did not feel safe. They did not feel that they could continue to live in Kosovo, and that obviously is a -- was a very significant reason for some of the people to flee. Those are the four reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, you said that the Roma federation helped you establish contacts. Perhaps others did, too, but let me put a specific question to you. Did anybody from the government of the Republic of Serbia or Yugoslavia give you any assistance in establishing contacts?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: No. No, not at all. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any representatives of the then-authorities of Serbia or Yugoslavia -- when I say representatives of the authorities, I'm referring to any representatives of the authorities at any level -- did any of these representatives, any such representatives, rather, attend meetings with refugees from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: No, never. Never. The only representatives that were there were from the Roma federation. Who were not being -- obviously who were not being interviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And agreement to have these interviews conducted by you and the members of your delegation, was this an expression of their free will of the interviewees, or did anybody bring pressure to bear against them in order to have them grant interviews to you, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: No. It was completely voluntary. I -- obviously not everyone wanted to give interviews. We -- we could very well have -- we would have liked to have had more -- conducted more interviews. Not everybody wanted to, but those who did want to we interviewed. I think there was -- the desperation was so great that these people wanted to tell, wanted to give witness to what happened to them. They wanted to tell their stories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you get in touch with the Albanians from Kosovo with whom you had interviews at that time?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: That was also thankful -- we thank the Roma federation for that. That was through our connections with them that they organised that for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when we're talking about general impressions, about all these people that you talked to, what was indeed your general impression about the psychological state that they were in just before the interviews were conducted and while they were being conducted?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: They were, to varying degrees, in terrible psychological state. They were in terrible emotional state. Many of them had seen their fathers, brothers killed, other family members murdered. They themselves had been either tortured -- some of them had been tortured, some of them had simply been threatened with death. They were extremely afraid. They were nervous. They were -- they were desperate and often crying. In some cases. In other cases it was -- it appeared that they were stoic, but nevertheless extremely afraid, terrorised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of knowledge did you gain then?

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Excuse me, knowledge? Could -- I didn't -- knowledge about what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what had happened to these people, through the interviews that you conducted.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Well, we learned a number of things. We learned that the -- that in many -- that in almost all cases, whether they were Romas or Albanian opposition people or Egyptians or Jewish or Turks, we learned that they -- or Serbs, we learned that they had been -- that their lives had been threatened and that what we learned was that one of the obvious things that happened was that in the days immediately after the withdrawal of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Yugoslav forces and the arrival of KFOR forces, this facilitated the arrival on the scene in many towns across Kosovo where they had not been active before, the KLA and -- and really a mass -- a dark -- perhaps the darkest day in recent European history, the mass expulsion of maybe as many as 130.000 Romas and hundreds of thousands of Serbs and other -- other non-Albanian peoples. Certainly there was also at least the expulsion of at least 20.000 - we were told from our investigation by Albanians who were extremely knowledgeable about non-KLA Albanian political movements - that at least 20.000 Albanians had been forced to flee by the KLA because they would not cooperate with the Albanian KLA movement. They were considered traitors. They were not considered loyal to the -- if they were not -- if they were not loyal to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, by Albanian opposition people, you mean those Albanians who were not loyal to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer that's just been given relates to a period after the withdrawal of Serb forces, effectively after the allegations raised in this indictment. It's not concerned with the movement of people from Kosovo out of Kosovo, it's concerned with the movement of people out of Kosovo after the period of which this indictment is concerned. It seems to -- possible to argue that it's entirely irrelevant to this indictment. I can't see what its relevance is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What Mr. Nice says is not correct. Witnesses testify about events in Kosovo and Metohija, about the time that is relevant. What is correct is that after the war ended, they were interviewed, but basically they were interviewed about what had happened at the time which is relevant in your view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have to make sure that the witness gives evidence about the period covered by the indictment. KFOR and UNMIK, that's after the indictment. But he can give evidence about the interviews, people telling their stories as to why they fled during the war, but we don't want evidence about events after the period covered by the indictment. And some of what he just said did relate to that period. So let him concentrate on the interviews relating to the period covered by the indictment, why the people fled.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Certainly, Mr. Robinson. I'll make sure I do that. But I would like to draw your attention to the behaviour of the KLA to the Serbs and Roma and Turks and Egyptians and Roma. That's a question that has to do with all times. This is constant behaviour. That's what witnesses speak about all the time, and that is why I believe it is relevant. It's a permanent thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You've heard what I said. Bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall certainly bear that in mind, Mr. Robinson, rest assured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy, now we are going to look at parts of some of your interviews, although we handed in all of your tapes. However, before we start playing the tapes, I have to clarify certain matters with you beforehand. Tell me, as far as Albanians are concerned, Albanians who were interviewed, do you believe this should be dealt with in closed session, for the sake of their own safety and security, or do you think that we can deal with this in open session? Let me be quite clear on this: I'm not talking about the Roma, the Egyptians, the others. I'm just talking about the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: BARRY LITUCHY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's my opinion that it would be risky and we would be putting the lives of the Albanians at risk if this was -- if their identities were known. So I don't think that it would be wise to -- to do that, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No advanced warning of this. This is typically a matter that, if it was ever going to be raised, should have been raised, as a professional lawyer would have done it, in advance. I absolutely object to this on the following basis: If this evidence or material is going in and if it's going to go in as evidence, it's going to go in on the basis that presumably what is said by the people concerned is truthful. Now, we've already seen by material not yet admitted as evidence but in relation to the witness Andric, people may say one thing in interviews which they then explain later they never intended to say. If the material is put out publicly so that the people can see it, there is an outside chance that I may be able to deal with the people concerned insofar as they're not fully identified in the tape and find out whether they meant what it is said they said or what is shown they said. The things dealt with in private session, even that possibility to deal with this evidence is going to be denied me. So that this material -- well, first of all, simply to have a witness express the very generalised concerns that Mr. Lituchy has addressed without substantiating it by reference to any particular Albanian is pretty unsatisfactory, the Chamber may think, but it will have the effect of making this evidence beyond my ability in any way to test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lituchy --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- I'd like you to elaborate on the statement that you made, Albanians will be at risk. I need to have a more substantial reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I'll give you two reasons. The first reason is that the KLA functions classically as a fascist paramilitary organisation that is determined to destroy first and foremost its political opponents. That means kill. Number two, of the three Albanians I interviewed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There were just three?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three in this video, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say that one of them was already murdered by the KLA, and that's why I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this just a wild allegation or --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's a fact. It was reported in the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has there been any arrests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, any charges against members of the KLA for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it may be worth observing that of the other two, since the witness has now identified the one who is dead, the other two are prominent members of the community, I think, he will confirm, who are members of the provisional Executive Council, just like Mr. Andric himself. Why they should be protected from the public disclosure of what they said on some earlier interview entirely escapes me. While I'm on my feet, if there is any intention to adduce effectively the interview of a person who is dead, the Chamber will recall that Rule 92 bis was introduced following an episode before this Chamber in the Kordic case specifically to deal, amongst other things, with the mechanisms for introducing evidence of dead witnesses. This is not the way that was envisaged, nor is it an appropriate way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, apart from the question of timing, that there is no notice given of it, isn't this a matter that the Tribunal cannot ignore, the possibility that the lives of persons to whom testimony relates may be at risk?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not question of ignoring it. It's a question, if I may say so, of dealing with the thing properly. If these named prominent individuals have any anxieties, it is for the accused in the normal way, through his associates or through Mr. Kay or Ms. Higgins or someone else, to get from those witnesses their express desire to be protected in some way from risk. That hasn't happened. It's just speculation by this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did we not protect persons like this during the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I can't immediately put my finger on an example where we did, but what is quite clear is that wherever there was protective measure, especially in the case where the accused was so insistent that absolutely everything should be given in public, we were careful to dot Is and Ts in supporting requests for protective measures by inquiries made either contemporaneously with the evidence itself or very close to by investigators who contacted the affected party. We don't have that here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well I grant you that, that you did follow the certain procedures which haven't been followed here. But the substances of the matter still needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are prominent people. There is no evidence that they express concerns for their own position. If this material is heard in closed session, there's no way I can deal with the issue, either in cross-examination or by raising the material with the witness, I suppose. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why is that, Mr. Nice, if you know who the people are?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since you know who they are --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Since they're named here, now I know exactly who the witness is speaking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the difficulty then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, if it's closed session, I'd have to have leave to explain to them what's been said about them and identify to them the fact that they've been referred to in this way. But there's also, of course, the practical problem that we've encountered with the Andric evidence, that even if I go and find from them that they express contrary views or qualified views, how can I deal with it? Because as things stand at the moment, although I can probably put the fruits of such inquiries to this witness, I couldn't certainly get the material in as evidence, although that's something I'm going to address more generally in another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That may be a question of timing, as you know. What pages should we be looking at in this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think what the witness has in mind -- if you look at the index, you find the index, something headed Contents, and I'm grateful to Ms. Graham for having perused late last night the extracted compact disk containing what I forecast the accused will want to lay before you, numbers 5 and 17 on the list are what's going to be the subject of evidence, but it's number 17 which comes first on the CD. So you have to find number 17. Now, unfortunately, the pages aren't numbered. I'm sorry, I haven't got a numbered one. It's page 127. I'm grateful to Ms. Dicklich. And at page 127 -- I've got it here. What we have is three names, and it's the one in the middle who is dead, and the other two are alive. Now, you can then -- I'm not -- for reasons of caution I'm not going to identify them by taking you through the detail, but you can read for yourselves what is said. If you look down a few lines to the first question, "Please introduce yourself," then get answer. So we can see what the first person's role in affairs is. And if you go over to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, could you hold it a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To deal with what is virtually an application, protective measures, we will go into private session so we can deal with it more effectively. I will also hear from Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As indicated earlier, we are going to take the adjournment now, and we will resume this hearing tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m. -- oh, I'm sorry. We have another hearing tomorrow morning at 9.00. We will resume this hearing at 10.15, 10.15.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And last time -- last time you said 10.50. Is it 10.50 or 10.15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's 10.50, ten minutes to eleven. Thank you. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
